attribution.note: Zitron's own forecast in his own post. The Amodei line that follows is separate context, not the claim.

semantics.note: 'Will' plus 'at some point' is a firm forecast with no deadline. The proposition keeps both companies, the 'don't need and can't afford' pair, and the cause he gives (mistimed growth projections).

contract.note: The plain reading (committed compute that is surplus and unaffordable, shown by write-downs, cancellations or defaults) is the ordinary meaning. Excluding unsigned deals that were dropped is fair. Having one company count as partial is reasonable.

evidence.note: Fortune, Oct 26, on the S-1. Excess compute is listed as a risk, but Anthropic says its past problem was too little capacity. No realised surplus.
As of mid-2026 Anthropic had operating income and $112B in cash, so it could afford its commitments then. This doesn't rule out the open-ended forecast.
OpenAI dropped a Norway offtake that was never signed and moved to renting through Microsoft. The contract says this does not meet the claim.

reviews.rationale: This is a firm forecast with no deadline. Nothing in the packet shows either company writing down, cancelling, reselling or defaulting on committed compute because demand fell short. The current evidence of capacity limits and enough cash argues against it for now but cannot refute an open-ended forecast. So it is unresolved.

attribution.note: Zitron's own sweeping statement in his post.

semantics.note: It keeps 'only grew because' (a claim that the subsidy was necessary) and the VC-funded burn loop. The phrase 'unlimited VC money' slightly simplifies 'burn as much money as they wanted', but the meaning is the same.

contract.note: The result depends on whether this is a strict universal or a claim about the typical hyped startup. He supplied neither reading. Under the strict reading one profitable counterexample refutes it. The typical-case counterfactual can't be tested with public data.

evidence.note: Gamma: VC-backed, past $100M ARR and 70M users, profitable for two years, raised little. This contradicts the strict reading. The figures come from the company, as reported by Unite.AI.
Replit's CEO says it is gross-margin positive. That cuts against 'entirely unsustainable', but it is an unaudited company claim and positive gross margin doesn't rule out VC burn.
A competitor says Cursor ran at -23% gross margins. That fits subsidised growth at one leading company but doesn't test the claim that the subsidy was necessary.

reviews.rationale: The burn-funded, below-cost growth part fits Cursor (e3). The universal 'only grew because' fails against Gamma, which grew fast while profitable, and is weakened by Replit's positive gross margin. Whether subsidy was necessary for the typical hyped startup can't be tested. So the result is mixed: partly true for some leaders, contradicted as a universal.

attribution.note: The profitability claim is Cursor's, which he reports. The claim scored is Zitron's own denial ('I call bullshit') and the evidence he cites.

semantics.note: It keeps the denial and the 'can burn $2–3 per $1' detail. 'Some' correctly reflects 'multiple' customers and the modal 'can'.

contract.note: Reading 'profitable' as gross margin across the enterprise book is reasonable but was the evaluator's choice. His evidence is about individual heavy accounts. Picking Q1 2026 when he named no period is fair.

evidence.note: Restates Forbes' report of Cursor's claim that business plans are profitable. This is the claim he disputes, not independent proof.

A single anonymous source says Cursor's large-enterprise sales were gross-margin positive as of April 2026. It leans against him, but the period (April, not Q1) and the scope don't match, and it is thinly sourced.

reviews.rationale: No readable disclosure gives Cursor's enterprise gross margin for Q1 2026. The only counter-report has one anonymous source, describes April and covers large enterprises only. His own evidence comes from unnamed customers and can't be checked. The packet doesn't settle the claim.

attribution.note: Zitron's own statement about what happened.

semantics.note: It keeps 'just about every', 'had to' and the period after June 2025. The link to the priority tiers comes from the section heading he wrote.

contract.note: Reading 'just about every' as a large majority of startups that resell model access, and the period as June to December 2025, is fair and ordinary. Defining 'austerity' broadly helps him. The breadth threshold is the evaluator's choice.

evidence.note: Cursor moved its Pro plan from request-based to capped usage pricing in June 2025, citing token costs. One instance; it doesn't show how common this was.
Augment moved to credits in October 2025 because the old model wasn't sustainable. A cost-driven instance; one company only.
The Register quotes Augment's CEO naming pricing changes at Zed, Replit, Cursor and Anthropic. This suggests a trend among coding tools; it is not a survey.

reviews.rationale: The evidence confirms cost-driven tightening at several coding-tool startups (Cursor, Augment, and reportedly Zed and Replit) in the window. There is no representative data for AI startups generally, so 'just about every' can't be checked. The examples hold; the claim about breadth is unsettled.
